name: Sasak
confidence_why: no confirmed first-hand statement: the record's source was not confirmed
sweep_summary: Sasak (sasa1249) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant (final stress), with a carried-secondary Wikipedia quote as the deciding source. this search of works with stress in the title had one title item: Bishop 1998, 'The intonation of Sasak: an autosegmental-metrical analysis' (Austin ed., Sasak, Univ. of Melbourne working papers, pp. 23-66). It is relevant to word stress (Archangeli et al. 2020 cite it for the unstressed status of syllabic enclitics) but is a departmental working-papers volume with no open copy found: Peter Austin's site lists the 1998 volume without a PDF; Glottolog has no URL; archive.org, OpenLibrary and Melbourne's Minerva repository have nothing; Best first-hand statement actually read: Archangeli, Tanashur & Yip 2020 JIPA 50(1): 104-105 (Stress section, already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 check) — final stress including suffixes, f0 peaks and longer duration on the stressed vowel, syllabic pronominal enclitics unstressed; it confirms the catalog's classification and should replace the Wikipedia citation as the deciding source, with Austin 2004: 4 (held by the project, open at peterkaustin.com) as the primary behind the Wikipedia sentence.

new_statements.quote: Stress typically falls on the final syllable (Clynes 1995, citing Thoir 1979), including word-final suffixes, and is associated with f0 peaks during the stressed vowel. Pronominal clitics that form an independent syllable (when attaching to a consonant-final stem) are not stressed (Bishop 1998), as in /sapaʔ-k/ [sa.ˈpaʔ.ək] sapaqk ‘greet me’ (‘greet’ + 1.SG.OBJ), /rapat-m/ [ra.ˈpat.m̩] rapatm ‘your discussion’ (‘discussion’ + 2.SG.POSS), and /ndaus-n/ [n̩.da.ˈus.ən] ndausn ‘his/her/its shower’ (‘shower’ + 3.SG.POSS) (see Figure 12). [...] Vowel duration also appears to be longer in stressed environments.
new_statements.citation: Archangeli, Diana, Panji Tanashur & Jonathan Yip. 2020. Sasak, Meno-Mené dialect. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 50(1): 93-108. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0025100318000063
new_statements.locator: Stress section, pp. 104-105 (also p. 99 parenthetical and p. 103 on epenthetic clitic vowels; Figure 12 p. 105 shows f0 peaks)
new_statements.reading: Fixed word-final stress (suffixes count as part of the word; enclitics do not), confirmed instrumentally by f0 peaks and longer vowel duration on the final stem syllable; the only exception is a syllabic pronominal enclitic, which leaves stress on the stem-final (now penultimate) syllable. Same passage also at p. 99: 'Stress falls on the final syllable in Sasak, except for pronominal clitic syllables, where stress is penultimate.' Confirms the catalog's fixed-dominant / final coding and matches the independent first-hand statement in Austin 2004: 4 ('Sasak phonological words have a single stress which falls on final syllable'; suffixes 'are all part of word stress domain', clitics 'occur outside the stress domain').

audit.reasoning: The record codes Sasak as fixed final stress on the strength of a Wikipedia sentence (second-hand from Austin 2004:4), with no copies we hold, empty cite/loc/grade fields. For questions, Bishop (1998: 37) suggests that the primary indicator is an utterance-final high boundary tone".

sources.note: Title is intonation (AM analysis), but an AM analysis assigns pitch accents to stressed syllables, and Archangeli et al. 2020 cite Bishop 1998 specifically for the word-stress fact that syllabic pronominal clitics are unstressed (stress stays on the stem-final syllable). So it contains a first-hand statement on Sasak word-stress placement, at least for the clitic case; its main content is phrase accents and boundary tones.
